title: A chronological framework for atherosclerosis: from environmental pressure to clinical disease, with vascular aging as a cross-cutting dimension.
abstract: Atherosclerosis is a multiphase disease, yet contemporary cardiovascular risk stratification relies predominantly on calculators that estimate event probability within a limited pathophysiological window. Framingham, SCORE2, GLOBORISK and PREVENT capture lipid burden, metabolic parameters, and renal function, but they do not organize the chronological sequence of atherogenesis, assign measurable biomarkers to each stage, or integrate vascular aging. We propose CASCADE (Chronological Atherosclerosis Staging: Connecting Aging, Disease, and Environment), a conceptual framework that applies disease staging to atherosclerosis, organizing it into seven pathophysiological phases (F1-F7) preceded by an upstream environmental and behavioral pressure layer (F0), and spanning the trajectory from adaptive metabolic response to clinical cardiovascular disease. Each phase is mapped to a proposed dominant biomarker - from insulin resistance indices through apolipoprotein B, lipoprotein(a), and coronary artery calcium - and to a reversibility zone (largely reversible, transition, or stabilization only). Vascular aging - characterized by arterial stiffness, cellular senescence, epigenetic drift, and clonal hematopoiesis - traverses all phases as a modifiable cross-cutting dimension, with specific biological clocks applicable at each stage. The framework is developed through narrative synthesis of mechanistic, epidemiological, and clinical trial evidence, integrating current international guidelines and emerging evidence on biological aging and environmental determinants of cardiovascular risk. CASCADE complements existing risk calculators by providing chronological context for the upstream phases (F0-F3), where conventional tools offer limited guidance and the potential for disease modification is greatest. It is proposed as a hypothesis-generating framework, not a validated scoring system, and invites prospective evaluation of whether individuals traverse identifiable, modifiable phases of atherosclerotic disease - and whether integrating vascular aging measurement at each stage improves risk assessment and therapeutic decision-making.

title: Convergent ferroptosis and pyroptosis in MASLD-associated cardiac remodeling.
journal: Translational research : the journal of laboratory and clinical medicine
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects ∼30% of the global population and is associated with increased risks of heart failure (particularly heart failure with preserved ejection fraction), atrial fibrillation, and cardiovascular mortality. Despite well-established epidemiological links between MASLD and cardiovascular disease, the molecular pathways driving MASLD-related cardiac remodeling remain incompletely understood. This state-of-the-art mini review examines ferroptosis and pyroptosis as potentially convergent regulated cell-death pathways relevant to both the steatotic liver and the remodeling heart. Ferroptosis is an iron-dependent, lipid peroxidation-driven cell death that mediates hepatocyte injury in experimental MASLD and contributes to cardiomyocyte injury under cardiac stress. Pyroptosis is an inflammasome-mediated pro-inflammatory cell death executed by gasdermin D, which amplifies tissue inflammation in hepatic and cardiac disease. Direct preclinical evidence from a pressure-overload heart-failure model demonstrates ferroptosis-to-pyroptosis signaling through the ACSL4/ALOX12/12-HETE/NLRP3 axis; however, this cascade has not yet been directly validated in MASLD models or in patients with MASLD-associated cardiac remodeling. We therefore distinguish experimentally established within-organ mechanisms from hypothesized interorgan liver-heart links, highlight shared regulators including reactive oxygen species, the cGAS/STING pathway, and the NRF2 hub, and discuss translational strategies and evidence gaps that should guide future validation.

title: Pah in the era of obesity: navigating phenotypes of pulmonary hypertension.
keywords: Heart Failure With Preserved Ejection Fraction
abstract: Introduction Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vasculopathy whose phenotype has shifted over the decades from young women to older patients with cardiometabolic comorbidities. Obesity is among the most prevalent and clinically consequential of these comorbidities, affecting 24-40% of patients in contemporary PAH registries. Areas covered We review the epidemiology of obesity and its impact on PAH; the definition of obesity and the limitations of body mass index; the effects of obesity on adipose, cardiovascular and respiratory systems; its association with health disparities; the clinical approach to the patient with obesity and suspected pulmonary hypertension (PH), including right heart catheterization with provocative maneuvers and esophageal manometry; comorbid conditions and the obesity paradox; and management, including weight loss, PAH-specific therapy, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and sleep-disordered breathing. A literature search of PubMed/MEDLINE was performed for articles published from database inception to September 2026. Expert opinion Obesity has implications in the origin, symptoms, diagnosis and management of PH. Accurate characterization of PH in obese patients depends first on measuring and reporting pressures that reflect true transmural hemodynamics. Incretin-based therapy and activin signaling inhibition are promising therapeutic directions, but dedicated trials in patients with obesity and pulmonary hypertension are needed.
ids: title:pah in the era of obesity navigating phenotypes of pulmonary hypertension

title: [Mechanism by which disulfiram improves cardiac function in HFpEF rats via the GSDMD/Drp1 signaling pathway].
journal: Zhonghua xin xue guan bing za zhi

abstract: Objective: To investigate the role of the gasdermin D (GSDMD)/dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp1) signaling pathway in cardiac injury and mitochondrial dynamic regulation in a rat model of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). Methods: Twenty-four 8-week-old male Sprague-Dawley rats weighing 200-240 g were selected and randomly divided into four groups, with six rats per group: control group (regular chow and drinking water), HFpEF group (fed with 60% high-fat diet plus drinking water containing 0.5 g/L N ω -nitro-L-arginine methyl ester for 8 consecutive weeks), disulfiram group (intragastric administration of disulfiram at 50 mg·kg - ¹·d - ¹ on the basis of HFpEF modeling), and mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) group (intragastric administration of Mdivi-1 at 30 mg·kg - ¹·d - ¹ on the basis of HFpEF modeling). H9C2 cardiomyoblasts were used for in-vitro experiments and assigned to four groups: normal cell group (cultured in routine complete medium with equal-volume vehicle), model group (treated with 12.5 mmol/L high glucose combined with 0.2 mmol/L palmitic acid for 12 h), disulfiram intervention group (40 μmol/L disulfiram added simultaneously with modeling), and Mdivi-1 intervention group (20 μmol/L Mdivi-1 added simultaneously with modeling). Echocardiography was performed to assess cardiac structure and function of rats in each group; a non-invasive blood pressure monitoring system was used to measure arterial blood pressure of rats; an exhaustive treadmill exercise test was performed to evaluate exercise tolerance of rats; HE, Masson, and wheat-germ agglutinin staining were used to assess myocardial histomorphology, collagen deposition, and cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area; Western blot was used to detect the expression levels of GSDMD, cleaved GSDMD, Drp1, mitofusin (MFN) 1 and MFN2 in rat myocardial tissues and H9C2 cardiomyoblasts; enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was used to measure N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide and inflammatory factors, including interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-18 in rat myocardium; co-immunoprecipitation assay was performed to identify the interaction between GSDMD and Drp1 in myocardial tissues of HFpEF rats; immunohistochemical staining was used to determine myocardial GSDMD and Drp1 expression in rats. Results: Compared with the control group, the HFpEF group displayed a higher body weight ((364.50±20.98) g vs. (256.50±6.77) g), blood pressure (systolic blood pressure: (162.99±5.61) mmHg vs. (125.33±7.15) mmHg; diastolic blood pressure: (119.78±4.58) mmHg vs. (81.01±3.85) mmHg; 1 mmHg=0.133 kPa), left ventricular end-diastolic anterior wall thickness ((0.38±0.03) cm vs. (0.29±0.03) cm), left ventricular end-diastolic posterior wall thickness ((0.32±0.01) cm vs. (0.25±0.02) cm), left ventricular end-diastolic internal diameter ((0.78±0.03) cm vs. (0.67±0.01) cm), and the ratio of early diastolic mitral inflow velocity to early diastolic mitral annular velocity (24.65±0.95 vs. 18.97±0.68). The HFpEF group also presented more severe myocardial fibrosis, larger cardiomyocyte cross-sectional area, elevated myocardial expression of GSDMD, cleaved-GSDMD and Drp1, as well as an increased phosphorylated-Drp1 (Ser616)/total Drp1 ratio. Higher myocardial levels of N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide ((112.45±12.18) ng/L vs. (42.38±6.86) ng/L), IL-1β ((60.14±6.28) ng/L vs. (32.31±5.68) ng/L) and IL-18 ((82.52±7.11) ng/L vs. (56.77±5.02) ng/L) were observed in the HFpEF group than in the control group (all P P P P P >0.05). In-vitro experiments showed that, compared with the normal cell group, H9C2 cardiomyoblasts in the model group displayed higher expression of GSDMD, cleaved-GSDMD, Drp1, and phosphorylated-Drp1 (Ser616), as well as an increased phosphorylated-Drp1 (Ser616)/total Drp1 ratio. These parameters were significantly reduced in the disulfiram-intervention group relative to the model group (all P Conclusions: A direct interaction exists between GSDMD and Drp1 in HFpEF. Drp1 may act downstream of GSDMD. The GSDMD/Drp1/mitochondrial fission axis serves as a key pathway mediating inflammation and energy-metabolism disorders in the pathogenesis of HFpEF. Interventions with disulfiram and Mdivi-1 can ameliorate cardiac pathological alterations in HFpEF rats by regulating this pathway, which provides novel potential therapeutic targets for HFpEF.

title: Cardiovascular Autonomic Function and HRV in Healthy Adults of Rajasthan: A Cross-sectional Study on the Influence of Age and Gender.
abstract: Background Heart rate variability (HRV) and cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CARTs) serve as non-invasive clinical indicators of central autonomic network function and cardiovagal regulation. Purpose This study aimed to establish regional normative reference values for HRV and CART parameters in healthy adults from northwestern India to evaluate the modulating effects of age, biological sex and subclinical cardiometabolic risk factors. Methods This cross-sectional study evaluated 142 healthy subjects (74 males, 68 females) aged 18-70 years. Baseline vital signs and time-domain HRV parameters (standard deviation of normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) and root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD)) were recorded. Autonomic reactivity was assessed using deep breathing (expiration-to-inspiration (E:I) ratio), the Valsalva manoeuvre, isometric handgrip and orthostatic challenge. A high-risk sub-cohort ( n = 21) with subclinical obesity or elevated blood pressure was analysed. Adherence to Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines was maintained. Results The total study sample comprised 142 participants, including 74 males (52.1%) and 68 females (47.9%). The high-risk subset comprised 11 males (52.4%) and 10 females (47.6%). Resting heart rate was higher in females (74.6 ± 8.2 bpm) than in males (70.1 ± 7.6 bpm; t (140) = 3.39, p = .02), while blood pressure was higher in males ( p = .03). Time-domain HRV and reflex indices declined significantly with age ( p p n = 21), where autonomic parameters fell below the 5th percentile limits (SDNN = 25 ms, RMSSD = 18 ms, Valsalva ratio = 1.09). Conclusion Healthy adults exhibit an age-related decline in parasympathetic function and a female-specific cardiovagal advantage. Subclinical cardiometabolic risk factors override these physiological buffers, blunting gender-related protection and accelerating autonomic senescence.

title: First Report of Real World Utilization of an Activin Signaling Inhibitor in Patients With Severe Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension in the Middle East PH RISE-ME Study.
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) remains associated with substantial morbidity and mortality despite advances in combination therapy. Sotatercept, an activin-signaling inhibitor, is a novel disease-modifying therapy targeting pulmonary vascular remodeling. Real-world data from Middle Eastern populations remain limited. We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study evaluating the real-world effectiveness and safety of Sotatercept in adults with PAH treated at a tertiary pulmonary hypertension expert center in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, between January 2025 and September 2026. Clinical, echocardiographic, biochemical, and risk-stratification data were extracted from electronic medical records. Primary outcomes were changes in right atrial (RA) area and NT-proBNP. Secondary outcomes included systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (SPAP), TAPSE/SPAP ratio, 6-min walk distance (6MWD), risk profile, and safety. Thirty-six patients were prescribed Sotatercept, of whom 33 received at least one dose. Most patients were female (80.6%), with a mean age of 55 years. Significant reductions occurred in RA area (- 2.67 cm 2 ; 95% CI, -4.16 to -1.18; p p p = 0.031). TAPSE increased significantly (+ 0.25 cm; 95% CI, 0.17 to 0.33; p p < 0.001). Patients improved by at least one risk category. The 6MWD did not change significantly. Treatment was well tolerated, with no adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation or death; two all-cause deaths occurred during follow-up. In this real-world Middle Eastern PAH cohort, Sotatercept was associated with improved right-heart remodeling, NT-proBNP, and risk profile, with acceptable short-term safety. These findings complement trial evidence and provide early regional support for activin pathway inhibition in routine practice.
ids: title:first report of real world utilization of an activin signaling inhibitor in patients with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension in the middle east ph rise me study

title: SGLT2 Inhibitor Therapy and Risk of Incident Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With HFpEF and Type 2 Diabetes.
keywords: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
abstract: Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) frequently coexists with Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction, particularly in patients with Type 2 Diabetes, due to shared cardiometabolic and inflammatory mechanisms. Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have demonstrated cardiovascular benefit in HFpEF, but data regarding prevention of incident AF remain limited. Objectives To evaluate the association between SGLT2 inhibitor therapy and incident atrial fibrillation/flutter in patients with HFpEF and diabetes mellitus. Methods We performed a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study using the TriNetX Research Network. Adults aged ≥18 years with HFpEF and diabetes mellitus receiving oral antihyperglycemic therapy were identified. Patients receiving SGLT2 inhibitors were matched 1:1 with those receiving Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors. The primary outcome was incident AF/flutter. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality, ischemic stroke, and composite major adverse cardiovascular events (cMACE; all-cause mortality, ischemic stroke, or acute myocardial infarction). Associations were assessed using hazard ratios (HRs) and risk ratios (RRs). Results After propensity matching, 37,108 patients were included (18,554 per group). Compared with DPP4 inhibitor therapy, SGLT2 inhibitor use was associated with lower incidence of AF/flutter (17.8% vs 19.2%; HR 0.84, RR 0.93), all-cause mortality (12.5% vs 21.4%; HR 0.53, RR 0.59), ischemic stroke (7.4% vs 8.7%; HR 0.78, RR 0.85), and cMACE (24.4% vs 33.0%; HR 0.66, RR 0.74). Conclusions In patients with HFpEF and diabetes mellitus, SGLT2 inhibitor therapy was associated with lower rates of incident AF/flutter and adverse cardiovascular outcomes, supporting a potential role for SGLT2 inhibitors in modifying arrhythmic risk in addition to established cardiometabolic benefits.

title: ACTIVIN A PROMOTES PROGRESSION OF PANCREATITIS INTO PANCREATIC CANCER.
journal: Transactions of the American Clinical and Climatological Association
abstract: The five-year survival rate for pancreatic cancer patients remains at 13%. Acute pancreatitis and chronic pancreatitis are risk factors for developing pancreatic cancer, suggesting a strong inflammatory role for disease initiation. Recently, we found that activin a (activin), a TGFβ superfamily member, drives inflammation in acute pancreatitis via recruitment of macrophages and activation of neutrophils. Here, we expand our studies in pancreatic cancer in the setting of inflammation and activin signaling. We performed digital spatial profiling (DSP) on a tissue section of human chronic pancreatitis with suspicion of pancreatic cancer to quantify more than 50 proteins relative to activin expression in situ. We found that activin co-localization is associated with reduced T cell activation and increased MAPK and PI3K signaling. These data suggest a previously underappreciated immunomodulatory role for activin in the setting of pancreatic cancer.
